meta_description: Inflation is just a tax — a plain-language explainer on government borrowing, bonds, and how inflation quietly takes purchasing power without a vote.
headline: Inflation Is Just a Tax — Once You See It, You Can't Unsee It

paragraphs.text: When you and I run out of money, the party stops.
Max out the card, the collectors start calling, and eventually someone shows up to repossess the car.
Governments do not play by those rules.

When a government spends more than it collects in tax — and most of them do, most of the time — it does not go bankrupt or sell the car. It reaches up its sleeve and pulls out the one ace card you and I will never be dealt. It simply borrows more.

The way it borrows is called a “bond,” which sounds fancier than it is. Strip away the financial jargon and a bond is just an IOU with an interest rate stuck on. Lend me a hundred bucks today, and I'll pay you back later with a bit on top. You hand over money. They hand over a promise. That is the whole deal.

The world's biggest economies run on a very formal version of borrowing twenty dollars off your mate until payday — except payday keeps getting pushed back, and the mate is you. And increasingly, your kids.

This is not small money. The United States is on track to borrow around $2 trillion this year alone, on top of a national debt already past $40 trillion. Picture a typical household earning $80,000 that somehow spends $98,000 every year for decades, and just borrows the difference while everyone politely agrees not to mention it. That is the operating model Michael Burry (of The Big Short) has called a Ponzi scheme.
Here is the sleight of hand.

The spending lands now. Roads get built, cheques get posted, everybody feels a bit richer. But the bill lands on whoever is around when the bond falls due — often a generation that was in nappies when the money was spent, or not even born yet. Buy now, pay later… except someone else pays, and they never got a vote.
Inflation really bites when the central bank lends a hand, quietly switching on the money printer to hoover up the new debt. Economists call it “monetising the deficit.” I call it printing inflation.

Now you genuinely have more dollars in the economy without producing more actual stuff. Same number of loaves, but more money chasing them — so the price of bread goes up. Not difficult arithmetic. We watched it in 2021, when pandemic spending was waved through by an obliging central bank and inflation ripped higher than it had in decades.
And that is the genius of it, if you can admire the magic trick while it picks your pocket.

Inflation is just a tax. It quietly shaves purchasing power off every dollar you own — the ones in your account and the ones you were counting on for retirement. But unlike income tax or the GST, nobody voted for it. No bill. No debate. No line on your payslip. Your money simply buys less each year. And because almost nobody really understands where inflation comes from, there is no one to blame.
The government spends like a sailor on shore leave. When your groceries cost more, it shrugs and does its best Shaggy impression: “It wasn't me.”
So next time a politician promises you the world and swears it will not cost a cent — because tariffs will pay for it, or a new tax on the rich will pay for it — remember this:
